tasks.description: Write 'Hello, World!' to a file called 'output.txt'. Then verify by reading it back and printing.
tasks.hint:
Write mode `'w'` creates the file if it doesn't exist and OVERWRITES it if it does.
`with open('output.txt', 'w') as f: f.write('Hello, World!')`
Then read: `with open('output.txt', 'r') as f: print(f.read())`
tasks.solution:
with open('output.txt', 'w') as f:
    f.write('Hello, World!')

with open('output.txt', 'r') as f:
    print(f.read())
tasks.walkthrough:
Mode `'w'` creates the file if needed and starts it empty, then the text is written in.
A second `open` in read mode gets the text back and `read()` returns it whole.

tasks.description: Write three lines to 'lines.txt'. Use a single write with '\n' between lines. Read back and print.
tasks.hint:
`
` inside a string creates a newline character.
`f.write('Line 1
Line 2
Line 3')` writes all three in one call.
When you read it back with `f.read()`, the newlines are preserved.
tasks.solution:
with open('lines.txt', 'w') as f:
    f.write('Line 1\nLine 2\nLine 3')

with open('lines.txt', 'r') as f:
    print(f.read())
tasks.walkthrough:
A single `write` call with `\n` between the pieces produces three lines in the file.
Reading it back and printing shows the line breaks as real line breaks.

tasks.description: Append a new line 'Fourth line' to 'lines.txt' without deleting existing content. Then read the whole file.
tasks.hint:
Mode `'a'` (append) adds to the END — it never overwrites.
`f.write('\nFourth line')` — the leading `\n` ensures it starts on a new line.
Then read the whole file with `f.read()` to confirm all 4 lines are there.
tasks.solution:
with open('lines.txt', 'w') as f:
    f.write('Line 1\nLine 2\nLine 3')

with open('lines.txt', 'a') as f:
    f.write('\nFourth line')

with open('lines.txt', 'r') as f:
    print(f.read())
tasks.walkthrough:
The first block makes sure the file exists with three lines, so this task works on its own.
Append mode adds to the end. The new text starts with `\n` because the existing content doesn't end with one.

tasks.description: Write a list of 5 fruits to 'fruits.txt', one per line. Use a for loop and f.write().
tasks.hint:
Loop over the list: `for fruit in fruits:`
`f.write(fruit + '\n')` writes each fruit followed by a newline.
Alternative: `f.writelines(fruit + '\n' for fruit in fruits)` does it without a loop.
tasks.solution:
fruits = ['apple', 'banana', 'cherry', 'mango', 'pear']
with open('fruits.txt', 'w') as f:
    for fruit in fruits:
        f.write(fruit + '\n')

with open('fruits.txt', 'r') as f:
    print(f.read())
tasks.walkthrough:
Each pass of the loop writes one fruit and a newline.
Reading the file back afterwards is not required by the task, but it's a good habit to confirm what you wrote.

tasks.description: Write a CSV-style file 'scores.csv' with headers 'Name,Score' and 3 student rows. Then read it back and print each row.
tasks.hint:
CSV (Comma-Separated Values) is just a plain text file with commas between values.
`f.write('Name,Score\n')` writes the header.
Then `f.write(f'{name},{score}\n')` for each student row.
tasks.solution:
with open('scores.csv', 'w') as f:
    f.write('Name,Score\n')
    f.write('Alice,95\n')
    f.write('Bob,87\n')
    f.write('Carol,91\n')

with open('scores.csv', 'r') as f:
    for line in f:
        print(line.strip())
tasks.walkthrough:
The header line names the columns. Each data line has the values separated by a comma.
Reading back line by line and stripping the newline shows the table as text.

tasks.description: Create a program that lets the user type lines and saves them to a file until they type 'quit'. Then print the saved file.
tasks.hint:
Open in append mode `'a'` at the start (or write mode if you want a fresh file each run).
`while True: line = input('>') if line == 'quit': break else: f.write(line + '\n')`
After the loop, re-open with `'r'` and print.
tasks.solution:
with open('user_lines.txt', 'w') as f:
    while True:
        line = input('> ')
        if line == 'quit':
            break
        f.write(line + '\n')

with open('user_lines.txt', 'r') as f:
    print(f.read())
tasks.walkthrough:
The file stays open for the whole loop. Each typed line is written with a newline, until the word quit ends the loop.
When the `with` block finishes the file is closed, and the last block reads it back.

lesson.intro:
Yesterday was mostly about reading. Today is about writing: several lines at
once, one item per line from a list, and a simple comma-separated table. Same
`open` and `with`, different habits.

sections.heading: Newlines are your job
sections.body:
`f.write()` writes exactly what you give it and nothing more. To get separate
lines, include `\n` in the string. You can write several lines in one call.
sections.code:
with open('lines.txt', 'w') as f:
    f.write('Line 1\nLine 2\nLine 3')

with open('lines.txt') as f:
    print(f.read())

sections.heading: Writing a list, one item per line
sections.body:
Loop and write each item with a newline after it. `writelines()` takes a
sequence of strings, but it doesn't add newlines either, so you still have
to include them.
sections.code:
fruits = ['apple', 'banana', 'cherry']
with open('fruits.txt', 'w') as f:
    for fruit in fruits:
        f.write(fruit + '\n')

with open('fruits.txt') as f:
    print(f.read().strip())

sections.heading: A CSV file by hand
sections.body:
CSV is just text with commas between values and one record per line. Write
a header line, then one line per record. Later in the course you'll use the
`csv` module, but it helps to see that there's no magic.
sections.code:
students = [('Alice', 95), ('Bob', 87)]
with open('scores.csv', 'w') as f:
    f.write('Name,Score\n')
    for name, score in students:
        f.write(f'{name},{score}\n')

with open('scores.csv') as f:
    for line in f:
        print(line.strip().split(','))

sections.heading: Writing what the user types
sections.body:
Open the file, loop reading input, stop on a magic word, write everything
else. Open in `'w'` mode for a fresh file each run, or `'a'` to keep adding.
sections.code:
with open('diary.txt', 'w') as f:
    while True:
        line = input('> ')
        if line == 'quit':
            break
        f.write(line + '\n')

with open('diary.txt') as f:
    print(f.read().strip())

watch_out: Opening with `'w'` and then reading from the same handle. Write and read are separate opens.
Forgetting the `\n` and getting all your items squashed onto one line.
Writing numbers directly. `f.write(95)` fails; it needs a string, so `f.write(str(95))` or an f-string.
When appending, remember the file may not end with a newline. Start the new text with `\n` if needed.
